data.title: AI is helping cyber defenders — and hackers — find vulnerabilities at a dizzying pace

data.title: Manuel Otto, German video game creator, dies in apparent livestreamed suicide
data.description: German video game designer and influencer Manuel Otto apparently died by suicide while he was livestreaming on Twitch, according to the streaming platform and his colleagues. He was 30. Otto was a 14-year-old high school student when he created his most famous game, “Stick Run.” The free Facebook game, later an app for Android and Apple, was played by tens of millions of people. His body was found Tuesday after authorities responded to reports of a blaze in an attic room on a property in the Bavarian village of Breitbrunn am Chiemsee, Bavarian police said in a statement to NBC News. “The fire was quickly extinguished thanks to the courageous intervention of a resident,” police said. “Despite the resident’s courageous intervention, it was too late to save one person still inside the apartment.” Colleagues confirmed his death on social media. “It is with a heavy heart that we confirm and announce the passing of our creator, developer, and fellow Stick Runner, Marc-Manuel Alexander Otto,” the Stick Run Team posted Wednesday on Facebook. An earlier post from the Stick Run Team said Otto “appeared to take his own life” in a livestream. Videos of the livestream later posted online appear to show Otto setting himself on fire. Meanwhile, a Twitch spokesperson said in an emailed statement that Twitch “moved quickly to remove the channel and Video on Demand (VOD) to prevent it from being viewed by others.” “What took place is horrible, and the mental health and wellbeing of our community matters deeply to us,” the spokesperson said. “We encourage anyone who may be struggling to seek support.” Otto launched his signature game, in which players control a stick figure running through obstacle courses, on Facebook in 2010. Since then, “Stick Run” has been played by more than 43 million people worldwide, according to Dexerto, a digital media company that covers video games. “Thank you, Manuel, for being a part of our childhood,” the Stick Run Team said in its post. “You will never be forgotten.” If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or chat live at 988lifeline.org. You can also visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional support.

data.title: Deciding with fake images: More candidates are using AI in political ads to get your vote
data.description: South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette appears distressed in a gloomy room as she undergoes a polygraph test that ends with the lie detector catching fire. Although the video clarifies that the “dramatizations” in this political ad are generated with artificial intelligence, some voters still asked her whether what they saw was real, Evette told Noticias Telemundo. At first, Evette said she thought, “This is ridiculous, right? Like, nobody could possibly believe this?” Later, as she traveled the state during her campaign to become the Republican gubernatorial nominee — a race she lost in June to Attorney General Alan Wilson — she said she encountered voters who were confused about the video’s veracity. “On the campaign trail, I would have people ask me, like, ‘Oh my gosh, did they really make you take a lie-detector test?’” Evette said. She then had to explain to them that it never happened and it was an AI-generated fake ad. “So you almost think it’s a joke and you kind of laugh at it, until you realize that there is a group of people out there that can’t tell the difference,” she said, “and then start to question if what they’re saying may be true.” Evette is not the only one whose image was manipulated in the lead-up to the midterm elections. The Wesleyan Media Project, a group of experts that tracks political propaganda in campaigns, identified at least 220 ads produced or enhanced with artificial intelligence by candidates or political action committees this election cycle. They cost just under $137 million. It’s a significant leap in the use of this technology compared to 2024, when the investment in AI was less than $50,000 during the presidential election. As of May of this year, the money spent on these AI ads was already $20 million. “We really saw the growth in AI ads over the summer,” Travis Ridout, a professor at Washington State University and one of the project directors, told Noticias Telemundo. “A lot of them were connected with closely fought primary races.” The lieutenant governor of South Carolina saw two videos of herself generated with artificial intelligence, or deepfakes, but she also shared one that falsely depicted her opponent, Alan Wilson, rejecting a call from President Donald Trump. According to Evette, her campaign used artificial intelligence after the ads featuring her circulated. “But we said it, ‘This ad is AI-generated,’” she said. The videos targeting Evette are said to have been paid for by a PAC; the one released against her opponent was funded by the lieutenant governor’s campaign. A request for comment sent to Wilson was not immediately returned. In response to a query from Noticias Telemundo on social media, nearly 40 people said they had seen political ads generated with artificial intelligence. Some admitted that they have difficulty distinguishing them. “And that could be deceptive; voters could be basing their decisions on falsehoods in that case,” Ridout said. “That’s, I think, what’s most concerning from a democratic perspective.” In the absence of a federal law regulating them, the responsibility falls to local governments, said Ridout, who estimates that about 30 states have some type of rule or requirement regarding AI in political campaigns. Of the 220 ads analyzed by the Wesleyan Media Project, only 27% revealed they used artificial intelligence tools. The possibilities ‘are endless’ Candidates with smaller campaign budgets rely on artificial intelligence to compete with their rivals, Ridout suggested. “I think it’s here to stay. I don’t know that it’s going to go away,” said Evette. Campaigns “are extremely expensive,” she noted, and AI reduces many recording and editing costs. These tools could also “unlock” more creativity in political advertising, said Ridout, “which wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world.” He said the possibilities are practically endless and include satire. Among the ads he analyzed, he saw candidates emerging from a swamp, boxing against Trump, or appearing alongside physicist Albert Einstein, who died in 1955. “I do worry about the lasting impact of those images, even if people know that it might not be true,” Ridout said. He noted those images might stick in their mind when they’re voting, or it may even generate waves of misinformation that trigger violence. AI can “redefine” modern political campaigns, the Brennan Center for Justice, a nonprofit institute whose experts have analyzed the potential impact of this technology on democracy, said in an article. Mekela Panditharatne, legal adviser and director of the center’s Elections and Government Program, said that without disclosure, “generative AI use in political ads has the potential to distort perceptions of candidates, painting candidates in a flattering light or their opponents in a negative light.” During the Minnesota primaries, a deepfake circulated showing Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, smiling amid mountains of money. A spokesperson from her office said that although it didn’t stop them from winning the primary, there was alarm over the impact of the AI-generated video. “There is already too much distrust in our politics, and voters deserve to know what’s real and what’s not,” the spokesperson said. Minnesota is one of the states with AI regulations; in 2023, its Legislature passed with bipartisan support a ban on its use to influence elections. The AI ad targeting Flanagan elicited debate over whether it was unlawful or whether it was protected under the First Amendment. Artificial intelligence “should never be used to manipulate voters,” Flanagan’s spokesperson stated. A matter of transparency At least two federal bills to regulate AI in politics are pending discussion and approval by lawmakers. One seeks to ensure that advertisements have conspicuous notices that artificial intelligence tools have been used; the other attempts to prohibit this technology “to generate materially deceptive content falsely depicting federal candidates in political ads to influence federal elections.” Although local regulations exist, some candidates still violate them, according to Panditharatne from the Brennan Center. “I think those laws have not had as strong a deterrent effect as we would like,” she said, making a point for the need of a universal federal standard. When designing any law, legislators take into account the First Amendment, which protects, among other rights, freedom of speech, religion and the press. Laws that are “carefully tailored” could withstand scrutiny under the First Amendment, Panditharatne explained. AI can also be used to create “forms of commentary or art,” such as parodies or satire. In the ads analyzed by Noticias Telemundo, the form and content indicating it was done with AI varied; there were differences ranging from the text size to the wording. One, for example, stated, “This ad contains digitally generated content,” while another referred to it as “dramatizations.” In some, the warning appeared at the end, and in others, it was omitted altogether. The use of AI in political propaganda concerns both Democrats and Republicans, according to Ridout. Candidates from both parties have been targeted by deepfakes, “and they don’t like that.” He thinks next year there could be consensus in Congress to impose some national standards. Republicans use more AI Republican-backed PACs and GOP candidates appear more willing to invest in these tools than Democrats and independents, according to a review by the Wesleyan Media Project. It found that 81% of the 220 ads identified were funded by Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups. Another 12% were from pro-Democrat sponsors. The remaining ads were sponsored by independent candidates or groups weighing in on issues that were not ostensibly partisan. Although Ridout said he has no explanation for this marked difference, he believes the key may lie in each party’s voters. Democratic voters, he said, tend to be “more in favor” of government regulation and perhaps Democrats may be more constrained by their own voters in terms of what they are willing to do, as opposed to Republicans. If a candidate “goes too far” in an ad against their opponent, they may also face backlash and criticism, he said. However, he noted that PACs, which typically fund their own ads, have less accountability to the public, “and I think they might be more likely to cross some lines,” he added. In some of the advertisements during this election cycle, AI was used for aesthetic enhancements, such as improving image quality or dramatizing events in the candidate’s life. But in others, it was used to criticize candidates by falsely portraying them alongside immigrants, trans people or drag queens as these groups have become greater targets. “That’s worrying,” Ridout said. There are also political figures or people who appear more frequently in AI ads; Trump’s image is often artificially used to suggest that he supports or endorses a candidate. New York Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is “a favorite among Republican advertisers,” the study found. AOC appeared in at least five altered videos that were negative portrayals. Noticias Telemundo requested comment from her office but has not yet received a response. The states that used AI the most in political campaigns were Oklahoma and Texas, the Wesleyan Media Project found. ‘Very dishonest’ In Louisiana, the Republican Senate primaries heated up after the release of AI-generated videos pitting Rep. Julia Letlow against State Treasurer John Fleming. Fleming said he saw between five and six videos with his AI-generated image and believed that they influenced Letlow’s victory. In one ad, reviewed by Noticias Telemundo, Fleming appears driving a bus with a Mexican flag, falsely suggesting that he was transporting immigrants from the southern border to U.S. territory. Fleming denounced the ads as “highly dishonest” and deceptive, as they showed him endorsing policies that he has never supported. They were also designed “to make you look unattractive physically,” he said. Although he acknowledged that those aspiring to public office are exposed to criticism and scrutiny — and that lies are also spread without AI — he insisted that political ads must be based on “truths.” His constituents were “very upset” about the videos, Fleming said, and although he said he tried to convince them that they were fake, “when you are outspent by a ratio of 20 to one, your voice is not heard.” In an interview with a local station, Letlow distanced herself from the AI ads targeting Fleming, claiming they were from PACs with which she had no connection and indicated that she was “not a fan” of AI in political campaigns. She also criticized Fleming for sharing on his social media an AI-generated video of herself in which she can be heard talking about her husband, Luke Letlow, who died from Covid complications days before he was to take office as a representative of Louisiana’s 5th Congressional District. Letlow now occupies that seat after a special election. Letlow has said that Fleming “crossed the line” with the AI-generated ad. “Releasing this video is shameful and indefensible. The family is off-limits, period,” she said. Her office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. When asked about the video, Fleming said that “the ad was from someone else, and all I did was post it temporarily, but it was actually very accurate.” Other Republican figures in the state asked Fleming to remove it. Ultimately, the person who created it was the one who deleted it, according to Fleming. Deny, deny, deny Given the growing popularity of artificial intelligence in the political arena, candidates will have to dedicate increasing amounts of time to debunk AI-generated advertisements circulating against them, according to Ridout. This is especially true as the technology advances to the point where it becomes more difficult to distinguish what is real, and people doubt everything they see. Both Evette in South Carolina and Fleming in Louisiana said it’s necessary to have safeguards to distinguish and clearly mark this content. “I don’t think that AI is the issue per se,” said Fleming, who mentioned that there were ads generated with this tool that supported his campaign using humor. “I think it’s whether you use AI in a productive and positive and truthful way.” Doubting some candidates is not “intrinsically bad,” Panditharatne of the Brennan Justice Center said, but the issue is the corrosive effect of distrusting electoral processes or institutions. Another risk to democracy, Panditharatne pointed out, is that some politicians will dismiss truths in what is known as the liar’s dividend. This means “disregarding or rejecting credible and authentic evidence by attempting to discredit it as false or AI-generated.” To combat that, digital literacy initiatives are necessary to encourage voters to carefully analyze what they consume without denying the reality of everything they see, Panditharatne said, since “that’s not healthy either.” An earlier version of this story was first published in Noticias Telemundo.

data.title: The Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders are unionizing
data.description: America’s highest-profile cheerleading squad has won a victory of its own: The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders have formed a union. The union is believed to be the first in the nation among all pro-sports cheerleading squads, outside of a short-lived effort by the Buffalo Bills’ “Buffalo Jills” in the mid-1990s. The Dallas cheerleaders’ bargaining unit has already been recognized by the Dallas Cowboys, according to a brief joint press release issued Friday by the team and the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association. The agreement came after “meaningful discussion” between the two sides, the release said. The next step will be bargaining for an official contract for the cheerleaders. The squad currently consists of 36 active members, though it is not clear how many will be officially represented by the union. “The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders are an esteemed part of the Cowboys organization, deeply respected for their talent and dedication they exhibit,” the two groups said in the release. Representatives for the Cheerleaders Association, which represents the squad, and the Dallas Cowboys did not immediately respond to requests for additional comment. The announcement comes in the wake of a multiseason Netflix series, “America’s Sweethearts,” that has documented the ups and downs of the cheerleaders’ on- and offseason lives. The attention brought by the series helped earn them a 400% raise for the 2025 season, with some veteran dancers slated to receive more than $75 an hour, according to a New York Times report. An earlier lawsuit by a former cheerleader had accused the Cowboys of paying her less than minimum wage. The team ended up settling the suit. During the Cowboys’ 1990s heyday, the cheerleaders made as little as $15 per game, according to The Dallas Morning News. The squad dates to 1961 but didn’t professionalize until the early 1970s, when Cowboys President Tex Schramm hired local choreographer Texie Waterman, who helped come up with the squad’s trademark star-spangled outfit that is still worn today.

data.title: Trump administration cancels some Canada tariffs, Sen. Susan Collins says
data.description: The Trump administration has granted tariff exemptions on some Canadian products, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who’s facing a tough re-election battle in Maine, said Friday. The move is an implicit acknowledgement that President Donald Trump’s signature trade policy could be hurting Republican candidates running in the Nov. 3 midterm election. Polls show Democrats have a solid chance to win majorities in both the House and Senate. The White House, Commerce Department and U.S. Trade Representative’s office didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. The canceled tariffs include 50% duties on some agricultural and forestry items. These duties were applied to Canada after the country withdrew from trade negotiations with the Trump administration in late August. Collins announced the news on social media: “I am pleased to have secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers.” She said that plastic boxes, crates, packing materials, refrigeration equipment, sealing and labeling machinery, packing equipment, film, foil and seaweed products were some of the other products getting exemptions. Collins said that many “farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.” Trump has repeatedly said “there’s nothing they have that we need” from Canada. “We have everything,” Trump said in September. Collins’ announcement did not mention Trump, only top administration officials such as U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. “I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner,” Collins said. Other Republicans have broken with Trump’s most well-known economic policy too. Mike Rogers, running for a Senate seat in Michigan told NBC News last week that he would like to see the trade war with Canada “wrapped up.” After U.S. officials made what Prime Minister Mark Carney called “unfair” and “uneconomic” demands, the U.S. hit Canada with two waves of tariffs, the second of which included the 50% duties. On Sept. 28, Trump predicted that Carney would be removing tariffs. “I think what’s going to happen is over the next three or four weeks, they’re going to come to us, and they’re going to say, ‘we’re going to get rid of all the tariffs,’” the president said. “We’re going to win everything,” Trump predicted. “They’re going to come in, and they’re going to say, ‘Sir, we are sorry.’” Asked about Trump’s prediction a day later, Carney laughed during a press conference, adding that he had no additional comment to make. Carney has stood steady in the face of repeated verbal attacks from Trump since the trade war kicked off in August. As Trump has ramped up social media attacks, Carney has turned to the rest of the world, opening up Canada’s economy to China, India, and the United Kingdom. Next week, Carney is set to reach a historic agreement with the European Union over the terms of becoming the bloc’s first-ever “associate member” during an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal. The European Union’s 27 member states collectively are the world’s single largest trading bloc and the union is the world’s third largest behind the U.S. and China.

data.title: U.S. airlines favor higher fares over fuller planes as fuel costs squeeze profits
data.description: U.S. airlines are increasingly willing to fly with empty seats rather than slash fares simply to fill ​them, betting that disciplined pricing and flight schedules will help protect profits at a time of soaring fuel costs. The strategy has delivered substantial revenue gains as demand has ‌held up despite sharp fare increases. Yet profits have still been squeezed as jet fuel prices surged roughly 90% since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February, forcing several major carriers to cut earnings forecasts. Executives at Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Alaska Air Group have emphasized protecting margins over boosting passenger volumes. Their resolve faces a test in 2027. Industry schedules point to more flying capacity, potentially intensifying competition for passengers even as fuel ​prices are expected to stay high and making this year’s substantial fare gains harder to repeat. “If fuel stays elevated, we have to continue to push yield up so that ​we can make a bit of money,” American Chief Financial Officer Devon May told Reuters on Thursday. Yield is the revenue airlines collect for each ⁠mile passengers fly. Six major U.S. airlines plan to grow domestic capacity 3.0% in the fourth quarter from a year earlier and 3.8% in the first quarter of 2027, a sharp acceleration from just ​0.2% growth in the third quarter, according to Airlines for America, citing Cirium data. U.S. air fares rose an average of nearly 23% year-on-year in the seven months through September, far outpacing the 3.6% average ​increase in overall consumer prices, according to Labor Department data. Airlines are still seeking increases. JetBlue Airways initiated a $10 one-way increase in domestic published fares on Wednesday, JP Morgan said, following a similar United-led increase the previous week that Southwest subsequently matched. United said it had nothing further to add, while Southwest said it does not publicly discuss pricing. JetBlue did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A different approach Airlines have long balanced fares against how full their ​planes are. But elevated fuel costs have made executives more willing to sacrifice occupancy and avoid discounts. United’s commercial chief Andrew Nocella offered an example during Wednesday’s earnings call. Its leisure load factor, ​a measure of how many available seats are occupied, fell 1.3 percentage points in the third quarter. Nocella acknowledged that the decline showed “a small amount of elasticity given higher ticket prices,” but called it “a trade we would make ‌every day.” American ⁠Airlines planes flew less full in the third quarter even as passenger yields jumped more than 18%. Finance chief May told Reuters the trade was deliberate. Delta has also been “managing the business for margins,” CEO Ed Bastian said. Across Delta, United, American, Southwest and Alaska, passenger revenue rose nearly $8.8 billion, or 18%, in the third quarter from a year earlier, while passenger traffic increased less than 1%. The divergence shows how much revenue growth now depends on earning more from each passenger rather than carrying more of them. Premium products and changes in passenger mix have also contributed to the gains. The Transportation Security Administration ​screened 2.9% fewer people at U.S. airports in ​the quarter than a year earlier, raising questions ⁠about whether higher fares are beginning to discourage travel. Limited capacity growth and the shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines have also weighed on traffic. Airline executives insisted that demand remains resilient. “Those higher fares are not causing an erosion of volumes,” Southwest CEO Bob Jordan told analysts, after the airline ​reported a nearly 22% increase in average passenger fares in the first nine months of this year. The 2027 test But record revenues have not been ​enough to shield profits from ⁠soaring fuel costs. Gulf Coast spot jet fuel prices have risen from $2.43 a gallon before the war began in February to $4.63 on October 20, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data. Delta and Southwest have cut their annual earnings forecasts, while American expects a full-year loss despite sharply higher passenger revenue. Airlines are now scrutinizing expansion plans. American intends to slow growth considerably next year, with May saying the carrier was reassessing whether additional flights ⁠would generate enough ​revenue to cover their operating costs. Southwest has pledged not to pursue growth at the expense of profitability, while United ​executives have cautioned that airlines’ published 2027 capacity plans may not materialize. Such restraint could help maintain higher fares. But flying less can raise operating costs per seat, while pushing prices higher risks discouraging travelers who have already absorbed steep increases. But airline ​executives say a disciplined approach on capacity can allow the industry to hold on to pricing gains. “We think these yield gains are very sustainable,” May said.

data.title: Etsy to restrict AI-generated content in effort to combat seller slop
data.description: Etsy announced new restrictions Thursday on AI-generated content on its platform, saying it threatens the integrity of its sellers’ work and leaves buyers exposed to fraud. Among the new stipulations: Patterns, recipes, or any other item that involves a buyer “putting in effort to achieve a finished product” cannot be created using AI.Sellers must include at least one unaltered photo of the actual item against a real background.Bot-generated listings are banned. AI-generated art can still be sold on the platform as long as merchants “Play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process,” Etsy said in a note to sellers. “Our marketplace only works when buyers and sellers trust each other,” Etsy Vice President of Customer Operations James Ossman wrote in a blog post. “Sellers need clear guidance and confidence that their creativity and craftsmanship will be represented fairly; buyers need to understand what they’re buying and the human involvement behind it. We know we have work to do to uphold this standard on Etsy.” Etsy hosts more than 5 million entrepreneurs, most of whom are women who run one-person businesses out of their homes, according to an annual company report. That distinguishes it from other major e-commerce platforms like Amazon and eBay, though it commands a fraction of those platforms’ revenues. As of 2024, Etsy hosted $10.9 billion-worth of goods’ sales, compared with about $75 billion for eBay and more than $700 billion for Amazon. Some buyers responded positively to Etsy’s announcement. “I can’t explain how infuriating it has been to purchase a crochet pattern, only to open the PDF and realize it’s fully AI-generated, doesn’t make sense, and definitely doesn’t match what the finished product should be,” creator Kara Lynne said on X. The dawn of advanced AI has led to an explosion in AI-generated sales content — and a growing backlash from consumers against what they see as AI slop. A recent social media trend among cafes and restaurants saw owners pledging not to use AI after egregious examples of AI-generated food images in the wild were shared on social media. Major platforms are responding to the growing discontent. Many, including Facebook and Instagram, now work to append labels to images or videos created via AI. Others, like LinkedIn, have added buttons allowing users to report AI-generated content. Snap has banned wholly AI-generated content from its recommendation algorithm, while Spotify recently announced it had removed 50 million AI-generated tracks from its platform. Ossman said Etsy would add a function similar to LinkedIn’s that makes it easier for users to report listings that include misleading AI imagery. He also said Etsy would be using technology to identify misleading imagery and fraudulent listings, with the goal of expanding removals of illicit listings in the coming months. “We’re actively working to address the questions AI raises for our marketplace,” Ossman said in the post. “This work is hard, and we don’t have every answer today. But I believe this is an important moment for Etsy, and that these initial steps are putting us on the right path.”

data.title: Russian diesel tanker heads to the U.S., the first since Trump’s deal with Putin
data.description: A tanker loaded with diesel fuel set sail Friday from Russia for the United States, the first shipment since President Donald Trump agreed a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release more fuel into the global market. Trump eased some sanctions on the Kremlin two weeks ago and has since waived more, reversing years of American policy despite Moscow’s ongoing illegal invasion of Ukraine in an apparent bid to lower prices ahead of the Midterm elections. The ship’s departure for the U.S. was confirmed by the Kremlin. The tanker, a Malta-flagged shipped named “Agioi Fanendes,” left a port in Russia’s Primorsk today, according to MarineTraffic tracking data reviewed by NBC News. The ship listed New York as its destination. Energy Aspects, a market intelligence firm, said that it had confirmed with its industry sources that the ship loaded up 298,000 barrels of diesel in Primorsk. The firm said that currently the ship plans to unload that fuel in New York. It is expected to arrive on Tuesday, November 10. The ship’s expected arrival would put it just after the midterm elections. Trump’s Republican party is on edge for potentially heavy losses in House and Senate seats its candidates are defending, driven in part by blowback from consumers facing soaring energy prices. Trump and his administration have scrambled to try to bring down those prices, which have increased in the wake of supply shocks stemming from the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars. Trump has taken a number of steps to warm ties with the Kremlin and pressure Kyiv to agree to end the war, drawing outrage from Ukraine and its bipartisan backers in Congress. “I believe there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has departed for its destinations and that further shipments will continue on a regular basis,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said early Friday. Crude oil was headed for a third straight weekly gain. Brent, the most important global oil benchmark, traded around $114 per barrel, less than $13 away from its highest point this year. Since the start of the year, the average price of diesel fuel has soared from $3.55 per gallon to $6.32, an unprecedented rise of 78%. Energy Aspect’s analysts said the impact of the cargo’s arrival would likely be “limited.” Diesel’s sky-high price has troubled economists more than the jump in the price of regular gasoline because, “the cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” as KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview. “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it,” she said. Currently, U.S. daily diesel demand is about 3.8M barrels per day, meaning that Friday’s shipment would satisfy not even a full day’s worth of usage. “Global distillate markets have tightened sharply,” said Bank of America’s head of global commodities Francisco Blanch in a recent note, adding that it signals “an acute scarcity of refined products.” Diesel is a distillate fuel, produced by refining crude oil. “Geopolitical disruptions are exacerbating that shortage as attacks on shipping around Hormuz make energy flows more difficult and costly, while attacks on Russian refining capacity further restrict product availability,” he wrote. Russia has historically been one of the world’s largest exporters of diesel. In September and for some of October, the Kremlin restricted the export of diesel fuel amid a Ukrainian campaign of attacks on its energy infrastructure. It lifted those export restrictions after Putin’s diesel deal with Trump. Easing sanctions on Russia to open up some previously-blocked diesel supplies was just the latest in a number of policy levers pulled by Trump. In just the last few weeks, the president has also signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road variety of diesel. The administration also pressured European allies, particularly Germany and France, to urgently release some of their diesel reserves. The administration has also reportedly pushed for a fresh release of crude and diesel reserves, though the International Energy Agency has rebuffed that request. Experts say that even all together, Trump’s actions will do little to help ease prices which have continued to trend higher. “Policy intervention can provide temporary relief, but there is no silver bullet for diesel,” Blanch wrote.

data.title: Trump promised $2 gas and cheaper groceries. Here’s what voters got instead.
data.description: When voters headed to the polls nearly two years ago, Donald Trump promised them cheaper groceries, gas below $2 a gallon and a wave of new manufacturing jobs. They elected him president — and got the opposite.
